title: India's Biggest Trade Deal Goes Live in Twelve Days. Here's What Changes for the Diaspora.
excerpt: The India-UK CETA eliminates tariffs on 99 percent of Indian exports, opens 137 service sectors, and ends double social security payments for 75,000 professionals. It enters force on July 15.
body:
India's most ambitious trade deal in decades is twelve days from going live. On July 15, the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement — known as CETA — will formally enter into force, dismantling tariff walls that have stood for generations and opening what both governments are calling a new era of commercial engagement between Asia's third-largest economy and Europe's second.

The deal is the most comprehensive trade agreement India has ever signed. Spanning 30 chapters, it goes far beyond conventional tariff cuts to cover digital trade, telecommunications, financial services, intellectual property, and — for the first time in any Indian bilateral pact — government procurement.

## What Changes on July 15

The headline number is staggering: approximately 99 percent of India's tariff lines to the UK will receive zero-duty access from day one, covering nearly the entirety of bilateral trade value. Tariffs of up to 70 percent on processed food, 21.5 percent on marine products, 18 percent on engineering goods, 16 percent on leather and footwear, 12 percent on textiles, and 8 percent on chemicals and pharmaceuticals — all drop to zero.

Going the other way, the UK is slashing duties on Indian goods entering Britain. Indian textiles, clothes, footwear, and select food products will face lower costs, potentially translating into cheaper prices for British consumers and stronger margins for Indian exporters. Whisky tariffs, a politically symbolic line item, fall from 150 percent to 40 percent. Automotive tariffs drop from 100 percent to 10 percent under a quota system.

India has protected its sensitive sectors — dairy, cereals, millets, edible oils, oilseeds, and apples are excluded from liberalization. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal called the structure "built on absolute economic security," noting that "stringent exclusion lists are actively deployed to insulate our sensitive agricultural and rural economies from import volatility."

## The Diaspora Provision That Matters Most



> **"The UK India Business Council projects the CETA will accelerate trade flows significantly, calling it "a historic milestone" in the relationship."**


For the estimated 1.9 million Indians living in the United Kingdom, the fine print that matters most is not in the trade chapters. It is in the companion agreement entering force on the same day: the Double Contribution Convention.

Under the DCC, Indian professionals on temporary assignments in the UK will no longer be required to pay social security contributions in both countries simultaneously. The exemption period has been extended from three years to five — a significant financial relief for workers and employers alike.

More than 75,000 Indian professionals and over 900 companies are expected to benefit directly. For an Indian IT consultant posted to London or a financial services professional on a multi-year project in Manchester, this means thousands of pounds saved annually — money that was previously paid into a system they would never draw benefits from.

"By exempting our professionals from double insurance contributions, we are protecting the financial interests of our talent pool," Goyal said.

## Services, Mobility, and 1,800 Visas for Chefs

The UK has extended one of its most comprehensive services commitments ever to India, covering 137 sub-sectors of export interest. Indian IT companies, financial services firms, healthcare providers, engineering consultancies, and education services will gain enhanced market access and regulatory certainty in the UK.

The mobility provisions are unusually specific. The agreement creates dedicated pathways for business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers, independent professionals, and investors. In a provision that drew attention during negotiations, 1,800 Indian chefs, yoga instructors, and classical musicians will receive dedicated mobility opportunities annually.

## Five Years in the Making

The agreement's journey from aspiration to implementation has been unusually fast by Indian trade negotiation standards. The groundwork began in May 2021 through the Enhanced Trade Partnership and the India-UK Roadmap 2030, which set the target of doubling bilateral trade to $100 billion by the decade's end.

Fourteen rounds of negotiations followed. The deal was concluded on May 6, 2025, and signed two months later in London by Goyal and UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, with both Prime Ministers present. The DCC was signed separately in February 2026. From signature to entry into force in under a year — what the UK government called "the quickest ever turnaround."

Bilateral trade between the two countries already reached approximately £47.9 billion in the four quarters ending Q4 2025, a 10 percent increase over previous years. The UK India Business Council projects the CETA will accelerate trade flows significantly, calling it "a historic milestone" in the relationship.

## The Strategic Context

The timing is not accidental. India has been aggressively expanding its network of trade agreements — the Canada-India CEPA negotiations are advancing toward a year-end conclusion, while trade discussions with the United States remain complicated by tariffs and trust issues. The UK deal, coming into force while American negotiations stall, gives India a concrete win and a template.

For the UK, the deal is also strategic. Post-Brexit Britain has been racing to sign bilateral trade deals to compensate for its departure from the EU single market. The India agreement — described by the UK government as giving British exporters "an immediate competitive advantage" — is among its most significant.

Prime Minister Modi called the agreement "a historic milestone" and noted it would "unlock numerous opportunities for Indian farmers, workers, MSMEs, startups and innovators." UK Business Secretary Peter Kyle said his government was "bringing our landmark trade deal with India into force as quickly as we can, because we want businesses and the public to feel the benefits immediately."

The India-UK Roadshow, a series of business events across Britain, begins this week to help firms prepare for the new trading terms.
